summary: Builds a working, approximate sense of common imperial units through key facts (1 inch ≈ 2.5 cm, 1 kg ≈ 2.2 lb, 1 litre ≈ 1.75 pints) used for estimation and sense-checking. Learners meet the ≈ symbol and the idea that these cross-system facts are used only roughly: the conversion factors are fixed but rounded for everyday use (e.g. 2.54→2.5, 2.20462→2.2, 1.75975→1.75), so answers are phrased as 'about …'. Relationships purely within imperial — pound↔ounce, stone↔pound, gallon↔pint, foot↔inch — are exact. Teaching anchors each fact to a familiar referent object and a dual scale, emphasises which unit is larger (and hence whether the count goes up or down), and treats conversion as scaling a constant multiplicative ratio rather than isolated one-off sums. Includes a hands-on/tool-based estimation activity, a static dual-scale fact activity, a check-and-practice activity, and vocabulary support; each with a distinct purpose and limits.
misconceptions: Treats an approximate equivalence as exact (writes 1 inch = 2.5 cm and cannot say the answer is only roughly right).
Confuses which unit is larger, so converts in the wrong direction (multiplies when they should divide, or vice versa) because the larger number of cm suggests a cm is the bigger unit.
Struggles with unfamiliar imperial vocabulary and relationships (e.g. knows feet and inches measure length but not that 1 foot = 12 inches).

activities.title: Dual-scale estimation playground
steps: Place a bag of sugar (about 1 kg) on a kitchen scale reading kilograms, then estimate its weight in pounds before checking.
Drag a pointer on a blank pounds dial to your estimate, then reveal the true value and compare it against a double number line showing 1 kg ≈ 2.2 lb.
Load 3 kg and watch both scales climb together; describe in words how the pounds number relates to the kg number (about 2.2 times), with a ratio/conversion table recording each kg–lb pair.
Use a ruler tool that overlays inches on centimetres: line up 1 inch and read off that it spans about 2.5 cm, then scale up (2 inches ≈ 5 cm).
Toggle 'is it exact?' to reveal the fuller value (e.g. 1 kg ≈ 2.20462 lb) and explain why the everyday answer is only 'about'.
activities.insight: Converting between systems means scaling by a fixed multiplier (pounds ≈ 2.2 × kg; inches ≈ cm ÷ 2.5), and because the taught factor is rounded the cross-system answer is used approximately, so it is phrased as 'about …'.

activities.title: Dual-scale fact set with referent objects
steps: Look at a dual-scale ruler (inches and cm side by side) and read off that a 30 cm ruler is about 12 inches.
Match familiar referent objects to facts: a 1 kg bag of sugar ≈ 2.2 lb; a 1-litre bottle ≈ 1.75 pints; an adult's thumb-width ≈ 1 inch (a child's is usually a bit narrower).
Tap each ≈ fact to reveal and read it aloud, saying 'about' each time.
After reading a fact, say aloud how you would scale it up (e.g. two bags of sugar ≈ 4.4 lb) even though the display does not recompute.
activities.insight: The key approximate equivalences become memorable when tied to objects you can picture and to a scale where both unit systems sit side by side.

activities.title: Estimate and sense-check practice
steps: Estimate on a slider: 'A 10 kg dog is about ___ lb' (expect about 22 lb).
Answer 'About how many inches is 15 cm?' and justify the direction of conversion.
Choose which unit is larger — 1 inch or 1 cm — and say whether the count of inches should be more or fewer than the count of cm.
Decide whether 2 kg of flour is more or fewer pounds than 2, and give a rough figure (about 4.4 lb).
activities.insight: Estimating and checking whether an answer is sensible relies on knowing which unit is larger and therefore which direction the count moves.

activities.title: Imperial vocabulary familiarisation
steps: Meet and say the imperial unit names: inch, foot, pound, ounce, stone, pint, gallon.
Match each unit to what it measures (length, mass or capacity) and to a familiar referent (an adult's thumb-width ≈ 1 inch; foot-long ruler = 12 inches).
Learn the exact within-imperial relationships (1 foot = 12 inches; 16 ounces = 1 pound) and contrast them with the approximate cross-system facts.
Re-attempt an estimation question after building familiarity.
activities.insight: Imperial units are often unfamiliar; knowing the names, what they measure, and the exact relationships within imperial supports confident estimation without a false belief getting in the way.

checkQuestion: A pencil is 15 cm long. Roughly how many inches is that — and explain how you worked it out. (You know 1 inch is about 2.5 cm.)
checkAnswer: About 6 inches, reasoning that each inch is about 2.5 cm, so 15 cm splits into 6 lots of 2.5 (15 ÷ 2.5 = 6); and stating it is only approximate because 1 inch ≈ 2.5 cm is not exact.
